0.0.n: Past form of 注文する, describing an order already placed.

0.1.n: Turns 注文した into a noun phrase referring to the things ordered.

0.2.n: Marks what was ordered as the topic, followed by the item names.

0.4.n: English lettering used as part of the product name BIGポテりこ.

0.5.n: Together with りこ, this forms the snack name ポテりこ; it is not a separate word here.

0.6.n: Completes the product name ポテりこ and has no independent meaning here.

0.8.n: Suggests particular care or attention went into this flavor.

0.9.n: 味 attaches to a food name to indicate its flavor.

0.10.n: Connects this ordered item to the potato chips named in the next line.

1.0.n: 揚げる means to fry; adding たて to 揚げ emphasizes that frying has just finished.

1.1.n: A borrowed food name; Japanese nouns do not need a special plural ending.

1.3.n: A Tokyo place name used here as part of the flavor description.

1.4.n: Combines with だし to specify the fish used for the stock.

1.5.n: Here it follows かつお to name a bonito-based cooking stock.

1.6.n: Links bonito stock and salt within one flavor name, rather than listing two separate items.

1.7.n: 塩 means salt and 味 means flavor; this completes the combined flavor description.

2.0.n: Refers to the two ordered items; adding も makes the reference include both.

2.1.n: With どちら, it includes each of the two items without exception.

2.2.n: A station name; 駅 means station.

2.3.n: After 東京駅, it indicates availability restricted to that location.

2.4.n: Here メニュー refers to food offerings, not the printed menu itself.

2.5.n: A polite sentence ending identifying both foods as station-exclusive items.

3.0.n: With の, it describes the familiar, regular version of the snack.

3.1.n: Connects いつも to ポテりこ so that it describes the regular version.

3.2.n: Together with りこ, this forms the product name ポテりこ.

3.3.n: Completes the snack name ポテりこ; it is not a separate word.

3.4.n: Marks the regular Poteriko as the thing that became bigger.

3.5.n: 大きい changes to 大きく before なる to describe a change in size.

3.6.n: Past form of なる; together with 大きく, it describes becoming larger.

3.7.n: English lettering forms part of the enlarged snack's product name.

3.8.n: Together with りこ, this forms the snack name in BIGポテりこ.

3.9.n: Completes the product name ポテりこ and has no separate meaning here.

4.0.n: Starts ポテりこ, a snack name split across three tokens here.

4.1.n: This is the middle of ポテりこ, not an independent word.

4.2.n: This token contains the final こ of ポテりこ plus の, which links the snack to its texture.

4.3.n: These expressive texture words suggest a crisp bite and a fluffy, tender interior.

4.4.n: Connects the expressive texture words to した so they can describe 食感.

4.5.n: With と, this form of する turns the texture expression into a description of 食感.

4.6.n: Refers specifically to how food feels when eaten.

4.7.n: Lists texture alongside potato flavor in the next line, without implying these are the only appealing features.

5.0.n: Written in katakana here, a common spelling choice for plant and food names.

5.1.n: Links the potato to the flavor being enjoyed.

5.2.n: Emphasizes the taste experienced and appreciated when eating.

5.3.n: With 楽しめます, が marks the flavor, together with the texture, as what can be enjoyed.

5.4.n: Provides the comparison point for 以上: the normal level of enjoyment.

5.5.n: After いつも, it indicates exceeding the usual degree.

5.6.n: Makes いつも以上 describe how much the texture and flavor can be enjoyed.

5.7.n: Polite form of 楽しめる, the can-do form of 楽しむ.

0.lit: What we ordered: BIG Poteriko, specially crafted potato salad flavor, and
0.tip: 注文したのは introduces what was ordered; the final と carries the list into the next line.

1.lit: Freshly fried potato chips, Nihonbashi bonito stock and salt flavor.
1.tip: たて after a verb's connecting form means freshly done, as in 揚げたて.

2.lit: Both are Tokyo Station exclusive menu items.
2.tip: どちらも means both when referring to two things.

3.lit: The usual Poteriko became bigger: BIG Poteriko.
3.tip: 大きくなった describes a change: 大きい becomes 大きく before なる.

4.tip: The final や links texture to flavor in the next line as examples of what you can enjoy.

5.lit: Potato's flavor can be enjoyed more than usual.
5.tip: 楽しめます expresses ability or possibility politely: you can enjoy it.
